Modified read with SLOOS insights:
- Policy stance: A hawkish pause. The FOMC held the funds rate at 5.25–5.50% and continued balance-sheet runoff, emphasizing cumulative tightening, policy lags, and vigilance on inflation risks. Inflation is easing but still elevated; job gains have moderated; tighter financial and credit conditions are expected to weigh on activity.
- SLOOS lens: Banks reported further tightening and weaker demand across key credit channels. For C&I loans, standards and spreads tightened with tougher covenants; banks pointed to funding costs, deposit outflows, liquidity positions, and declines in the market value of fixed-income assets as reasons for tightening. CRE lending standards tightened broadly amid collateral/value concerns and weak demand. Consumer credit also tightened, notably for credit cards and auto loans, with higher rate spreads, lower limits, and higher minimum FICO thresholds; approval rates fell. Residential mortgage credit remained tight, particularly in non-QM and jumbo segments, with subdued demand. Foreign banks similarly cited economic outlook and collateral values for tightening. These survey results reinforce that bank credit will be a drag on growth beyond the baseline statement.
- Risk balance: While the banking system is described as sound and resilient and inflation is easing, SLOOS confirms persistent credit restraint that compounds FSR-flagged vulnerabilities (CRE concentration, money market and Treasury market frictions). Net effect is more negative for growth and risk assets than a statement-only read, though not severely so given resilient funding conditions.

Net tone: modestly more negative than before due to SLOOS-confirmed credit tightening and weaker loan demand.
